title: Advanced passive structures
tagline: The passive isn't just be + participle — it also hedges, reports rumours and describes bad luck.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations (BELIEVED, THOUGHT, GOT, NEEDS, HAD, OBJECTED)
Reading & Use of English Part 2 — open cloze
Writing Part 2 — report/article: hedged, impersonal statements
Speaking Part 3 — reporting what is thought or said without naming a source
why: Beyond the classic be + past participle, C1 English uses the passive to hedge a claim (it is believed that…), to describe misfortune (get-passive), and to compress ideas into infinitives and gerunds. Use of English regularly tests the difference between having something done to you and something simply happening to you.

diagrams.title: Reporting a belief without naming anyone

before.text: People believe that the bridge is unsafe.

after.text: The bridge is believed to be unsafe.

steps: Make the object of the reporting verb (the bridge) the subject.
Add be + past participle of the reporting verb: is believed.
Follow with a to-infinitive — to be for the same time, to have been for an earlier one.

diagrams.title: have something done vs. have something happen

rows.label: Meaning
cells: Someone acts on your object — arranged or unfortunate
Something happens, performed by the object or another person

rows.label: Arranged example
cells: She had her essay checked by a tutor.
She had her students present their projects in pairs.

rows.label: Unplanned example
cells: He had his bike stolen outside the library.
He had his phone ring in the middle of the exam.

rows.label: Typical verbs
cells: break down, ring, walk in, happen

formula.ex: The bridge is believed to be unsafe

head: Pattern
Structure
Example
rows: It is believed that the company knew about the fault.
The company is believed to have known about the fault.
Two students got selected for the national final.
Nobody wants to be told what to do.
Being told off in front of the class was humiliating.
She had her essay proofread before submitting it.
The new policy was strongly objected to by the staff.

use.point: Impersonal passive: reporting what people believe, say or think, without naming them

examples.text: It is thought that the ancient trail once connected three valleys.
The results are believed to have been affected by a printing error.
examples.note: impersonal passive with a perfect infinitive

examples.text: She is said to be the youngest student ever admitted to the programme.
examples.note: impersonal passive with a present infinitive

use.point: get-passive: for something sudden, informal or (mis)fortunate

examples.text: Two of our classmates got selected for the regional science fair.
He got caught copying his homework and had to redo it.
The old gymnasium got demolished over the summer holidays.
Nobody enjoys being told they're wrong in front of the whole class.
The contract seems to have been signed without proper checks.

examples.note: need + -ing has a passive meaning: needs to be rewritten

use.point: have/get something done vs. have something happen; passive phrasal verbs

examples.text: We had the whole hall repainted before the graduation ceremony.
He had his bike stolen outside the library.
The proposal was strongly objected to by several parents.

watch_out.wrong: It is believed the bridge that is unsafe.
watch_out.right: It is believed that the bridge is unsafe.
watch_out.why: That introduces the clause immediately after the passive verb, not in the middle of it.

watch_out.wrong: The company is believed knowing about the fault.
watch_out.right: The company is believed to have known about the fault.
watch_out.why: After the impersonal passive, use a to-infinitive (perfect, if earlier), not an -ing form.
Something taken from you needs the causative have/get + past participle, not get + -ing.
Need + -ing already has a passive meaning here (needs to be rewritten); needs + to-infinitive would mean the essay does the rewriting itself.
The causative have needs a past participle, not an -ing form, when someone else does the action for you.

watch_out.wrong: The plan was objected by the staff.
watch_out.right: The plan was objected to by the staff.
watch_out.why: With passive phrasal verbs, the preposition stays right after the past participle.

dialogue.title: Rumours about the Cusco trip
dialogue.context: Nadia is writing for the school newspaper and checks facts about the cancelled Cusco trip with Miss Vega and Sofia.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: For the article — what can I actually say about why the trip was cancelled?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Be careful with rumours. It is believed that the bus company cancelled the contract, but nothing is confirmed.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: I heard the deposit got lost somewhere in the admin office.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: That's exactly the kind of thing that needs checking before it goes in print.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: So I shouldn't write that the money is thought to have disappeared?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Not without proof. The accounts are being audited this week.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Apparently the coordinator had her laptop stolen, and all the records were on it.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Wow. If that's true, this article needs rewriting completely.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Exactly. Write only what can be confirmed, not what is said to have happened.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Got it. I'll say the trip was postponed, and that an official statement is expected to be released on Friday.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Much safer. Nobody likes being told off for printing gossip.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Precisely — a good journalist reports facts, not what is rumoured to be true.

items.sentence: It ___ that the museum will reopen next month.
items.why: Impersonal passive: It + be + past participle + that-clause.

items.sentence: The suspect ___ to have left the country before the investigation began.
items.why: Impersonal passive with a perfect infinitive for an earlier action.

items.sentence: Their car ___ broken into while they were at the concert.
items.why: Get-passive: get + past participle, common for sudden or unfortunate events.

items.sentence: This proposal clearly ___ before we present it to the board.
items.why: Need + -ing carries a passive meaning: needs to be revised.

items.sentence: She ___ her parcel stolen from the front porch.
items.why: The causative have + object + past participle describes something, often unwelcome, happening to your possession.

items.sentence: Nobody enjoys ___ criticised in front of colleagues.
items.why: After enjoys, use the passive gerund being + past participle.

items.sentence: The new rule was strongly ___ by most of the staff.
items.why: Passive phrasal verbs keep the preposition right after the past participle.

summary: The impersonal passive (It is believed that… / X is believed to have…) reports what people think without naming them.
The get-passive suits sudden, informal or (mis)fortunate events: got caught, got promoted.
Passive infinitives and gerunds (to be told, being told) and need + -ing (needs rewriting) carry a passive meaning without a full be + participle.
have/get something done (someone acts on your object) contrasts with have something happen (an event simply occurs).
Passive phrasal verbs keep their preposition: be looked after, be objected to, be relied on.
